historical_root_cause: State-changing endpoints (/move, /reset) in the original incident accepted requests without verifying caller identity. No server-side authorization check was performed before game state was mutated, allowing any network-reachable client to alter live game state.
violated_security_property: Every operation capable of modifying game state must require trusted, server-side authorization before it is executed.

candidate_evidence.description: The /update endpoint (POST) calls game.update() directly without any call to check_auth() or any other server-side authorization check. game.update() mutates ball_x, ball_y, ball_vx, ball_vy, score1, and score2 — all live game-state fields — before the mutation is executed, with no identity verification of the caller.
candidate_evidence.contrast_with_protected_endpoints: /move (lines 23-34) and /reset (lines 41-47) both call check_auth() at their first line and return 401 if authorization fails, before any state mutation. /update performs no equivalent check.
game_update_mutations: game.py line 43: self.score2 += 1 (score mutation on miss)
game.py line 50: self.score1 += 1 (score mutation on miss)
candidate_evidence.unauthenticated_access_confirmed: test_app.py lines 45-47 (test_update_returns_success) sends POST /update with no auth header and asserts HTTP 200, confirming the endpoint is reachable and functional without credentials.

semantic_correlation: The historical incident involved state-mutating endpoints that trusted incoming requests by default and applied mutations without verifying caller identity. The candidate codebase introduces a new state-mutating endpoint /update that exhibits the identical behavioral pattern: it accepts requests from any caller, applies mutations to ball position, ball velocity, and player scores, and returns the updated state — all without any server-side authorization check. The mechanism is semantically identical to the original INC-042 failure: a POST endpoint that mutates live game state while trusting the request unconditionally. The recurrence is not based on keyword similarity; it is based on the concrete absence of any authorization gate before state-mutating logic in game.update(), applied to a newly added endpoint not present in the historical incident.
affected_behavior: Any client with network access to the API can POST to /update without credentials and advance the game physics tick, mutate ball position and velocity, and increment either player's score. The /update endpoint is semantically equivalent to the historical /move and /reset violations: it is a state-changing endpoint callable by unauthenticated callers.
existing_test_gap: The test suite includes tests that verify /move and /reset reject unauthenticated requests (test_unauthorized_move_is_rejected at line 36, test_unauthorized_reset_is_rejected at line 32). However, no test exists that verifies /update rejects unauthenticated requests. Worse, test_update_returns_success (line 45-47) actively asserts that /update returns HTTP 200 with no auth header, meaning the existing test suite explicitly encodes and validates the insecure behavior. There is no test that sends POST /update without an X-API-KEY header and expects a 401 response.
recommended_regression_target: A test named test_unauthorized_update_is_rejected should POST to /update without the X-API-KEY header and assert the response status code is 401. This directly mirrors the existing test_unauthorized_move_is_rejected and test_unauthorized_reset_is_rejected tests and would have caught this recurrence at introduction time.
